$comment: WO-07 section 2.2: every plaintext-capable component that is NOT our source
needs a source-to-digest binding, and a digest plus a stated Git revision is
not one. This file is the ledger of those components and the current state of
each binding.
It is deliberately a committed artifact rather than something a script infers.
The point of the gate is that an unproven link stays visible: a transparency
chain that quietly rounds an unverifiable link up to 'verified' is worse than
no chain, because it launders an assumption into an apparent proof.
status values:
REBUILT   option A. We built it from pinned upstream source and the digest
matched. Requires evidence.rebuild with the builder identity.
ATTESTED  option B. Upstream publishes signed provenance and we verified it
against a pinned identity. Requires evidence.attestation.
NONE      no binding established. This is a RECORDED GAP, not a pass, and
must appear in the release manifest and the public README.
registryProvenance   an UNSIGNED in-toto statement the registry publishes whose
subject is our pinned digest. It names the upstream commit
and so gives a rebuild something exact to compare against,
but it CANNOT satisfy a binding: its trust root is registry
push access, not an identity we pinned.
A status of REBUILT or ATTESTED without the matching evidence block is a
schema error, not a warning. See scripts/verify-third-party-provenance.ts.

components.role: Base image of the in-CVM L7 edge, which proxies customer plaintext after TLS terminates inside the trust domain
note: MISSING FROM THIS LEDGER UNTIL NOW, and it should not have been. The edge
sits behind dstack-ingress and proxies customer requests AFTER TLS has
terminated inside the trust domain, so it handles plaintext by definition.
WO-07 section 2.2 applies to it exactly as it applies to the node base.
PROBLEM 1, MUTABLE REFERENCE: CLOSED, and it was open. Every Dockerfile
using this base pinned the multi-architecture INDEX digest recorded above,
not a manifest. An index digest is immutable, which is what made it look
like a pin; it still resolves to a different image per builder
architecture, so two builds of identical source would differ with nothing
recording which ran. All six affected pins across edge, edge-acme,
edge-tls, egress, tlsprobe and venice-egress now name their linux/amd64
child manifest. Found by scripts/audit-base-image-pins.ts and held by
tests/unit/base-image-pin-platform.test.ts.
PROBLEM 2, CONTENTS UNVERIFIED: OPEN, which is why the binding is NONE.
A pinned digest makes the build reproducible and says nothing about what
is inside the image. Caddy's Docker Official Image is built from Alpine,
so option A means trusting Alpine's archive transitively, and option B
means provenance that Docker Official Images do not publish in a form
pinnable to a single upstream identity. Same shape as node-base-image.
MEASURED 2026-09-02, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME AS 'NOT DONE YET' AND ALSO NOT
THE SAME AS 'CAN NEVER BE DONE'. Read claimScope below for the exact
boundary; an earlier revision of this entry crossed it.
AnonRouter's public CI replayed docker-library's recorded invocation for
this exact digest, natively on linux/amd64, three times. Every argument
came from the deployed image's own SLSA statement: the git URL, the commit
fba28535, the directory 2.11/alpine, the alpine:3.23 parent resolved to
oisupport/staging-amd64@sha256:1beb0dc0, the tianon/buildkit:0.16 frontend
by digest, and the build arguments. The replay was additionally HANDED the
deployed manifest's own annotations, including the build clock, which makes
the test maximally favourable.
It failed, and the decisive part is not the failure against the deployed
image. Two IDENTICAL invocations, minutes apart on the same runner with a
cold cache, produced sha256:814143b2... and sha256:eec80ff0..., which are
different images. The PUBLISHED RECIPE is therefore not deterministic, so no
REPLAY of it can match a fixed digest, whoever runs the replay. That is a
statement about replaying this recipe, not about every possible route to a
binding.
The whole difference between those two runs is one file, /var/log/apk.log,
whose first line reads 'Running `apk add --no-cache ca-certificates curl
libcap mailcap` at 2026-06-22 20:09:02' in the deployed image. It is file
CONTENT, not metadata, so no timestamp-normalisation flag rewrites it, and
21 image-config history timestamps move with it.
The SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH branch was tested too, so it is not left as an
untested excuse: setting it to the deployed build clock produced
sha256:7a4b0434..., also not the deployed digest. Leaving the epoch unset
lets the clock move; setting it collapses the per-step timestamps the
deployed config records at sub-second precision. Neither branch can work.
AND THE ARCHIVE HAS MOVED, which is an independent obstruction. Against the
deployed image the rebuild differs in five paths that have nothing to do
with time: c-ares went 1.34.6 to 1.34.7 (libcares.so.2.19.5 became .19.7),
curl and libcurl were rebuilt, and lib/apk/db/installed records the new
versions. `apk add --no-cache` resolves against Alpine v3.23's live
repository, which is mutable, so the contents of this image were never
recoverable from its source after the fact.
NO QUALIFYING SIGNATURE EXISTED ON 2026-09-02, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED,
and this is the route that could change without anything on our side
changing: upstream can start signing at any time. No OCI referrer on
the child manifest or the index, no cosign .sig sibling tag, no GitHub
attestation under docker-library. Sigstore's transparency log DOES carry one
entry over this digest and it is unusable: a hashedrekord with a bare public
key, no certificate, so no subject and no issuer. Anyone can create one over
any digest. A checker that asked only 'is this digest in the transparency
log' would have passed it, which is why the check records the shape and not
just the count.
CONSEQUENCE FOR ALREADY-PUBLISHED IMAGES, recorded rather than left to be
discovered: ghcr.io/anonrouter/anonrouter-edge-ingress@sha256:4645b36c...,
anonrouter-venice-egress@sha256:c4508541... and
anonrouter-control-egress@sha256:bacb13dc... were built from the
PRE-REPIN Dockerfiles, whose git blob ids at commit c714b6f were
edge e12f911b, egress 000034b1, venice-egress 91635740. Rebuilding any of
them from the current source will produce a different digest. That is the
correct outcome and not a discrepancy to explain away: the edge has to be
rebuilt regardless, because its baked-in Caddyfile gained the receipt and
credential routes for prod5.

claimScope: WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES: replaying the recipe docker-library publishes for this
digest did not reproduce it, and two identical replays of that recipe disagreed
with each other, so the published recipe is not deterministic. No signature
meeting this project's option B bar existed for the digest on the date below.
WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH, and an earlier revision of this entry overstated
exactly here by phrasing a scoped negative as a universal one: this does not
show the digest is permanently unbindable. Upstream could publish a
qualifying signature, which would close
this with no rebuild at all; a party holding build inputs outside the published
recipe could produce evidence this run cannot; and this project could accept a
different kind of evidence after review. The claim is scoped to the published
recipe, the inputs reachable from it, and the measurement date.

obstructions.detail: Two identical native linux/amd64 invocations, minutes apart with a cold cache, produced sha256:814143b2 and sha256:eec80ff0. The published recipe is not deterministic, so no replay of it can match a fixed digest, whoever runs the replay.

/var/log/apk.log ships inside the image and its first line records the second the build ran: 'Running `apk add --no-cache ca-certificates curl libcap mailcap` at 2026-06-22 20:09:02'. File content, not metadata, so no normalisation flag rewrites it.
21 history timestamps differ between two runs of the same recipe, at sub-second precision.

org.opencontainers.image.created is derived from `env.SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH // now` by docker-library's meta.jq, and the recorded build set no epoch. The annotation is manifest bytes, so it is part of the digest.

`apk add --no-cache` resolves against Alpine v3.23's live repository. Against the deployed image the rebuild differs by c-ares 1.34.6 -> 1.34.7, a rebuilt curl and libcurl, and the matching lib/apk/db/installed entries. The contents were never recoverable from the source after the fact.

No OCI referrer on the child or the index, no cosign .sig sibling tag, no GitHub attestation under docker-library. One Rekor entry names this digest and carries a bare public key rather than a certificate, so it attests to no identity at all.

buildToolDependencies.why: the unpack stage runs dpkg-deb and ldconfig. None of its bytes reach the shipped image, every input it consumes is hash-pinned before it runs, and two independent CI jobs must agree on the output digest. A weaker exposure than an inherited rootfs, and not zero.

compatibility.comparedAgainst: the base the component runs today, same source, same policy

note: UNDEPLOYED CANDIDATE, INTEGRATED IN SOURCE. It proves nothing about the
digest above, and the schema refuses to let it read as though it did.
BUILT FROM scratch. The first version of this candidate was
FROM debian:bookworm-slim, which is a Docker Official Image with exactly the
unbound provenance of the image it replaces: the gap had moved down a layer
and the paperwork had moved with it. Caddy is statically linked, so the edge
needs no libc, no shell and no package manager at runtime, and there is now
no inherited rootfs to account for. inheritedBaseImages is empty and the
schema requires it to be.
WHAT REMAINS IS NAMED. The unpack stage runs on the pinned Debian image
because something has to run dpkg-deb. See buildToolDependencies.
DEBIAN WHERE UPSTREAM IS ALPINE, and that is forced. `apk add --no-cache`
resolves against Alpine v3.23's LIVE repository, which moved under the
measurement: c-ares 1.34.6 to 1.34.7, curl and libcurl rebuilt. Alpine
publishes no snapshot archive, so there is nothing to pin, and pinning exact
apk versions converts irreproducibility into breakage when they are pruned.
COMPATIBILITY WAS MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED. The harness builds the SAME
Caddyfile on the stock base and on this one and runs an identical matrix
under the real policy: read_only, cap_drop ALL, no-new-privileges, init,
three tmpfs mounts, the read-only evidences volume and mem_limit 96m. 24 of
24 checks identical, including every route class, the 404 invariants, the
credential routes that must not cross-wire, file_server browse, and shutdown
behaviour. A third edge with one route rewired is the control: the matrix
detects it, so 'identical' is not the answer of a matrix that cannot tell
two images apart.
TWO PRE-EXISTING FINDINGS SURFACED and are attributed to the deployment
rather than to this image, because they reproduce on the stock base: an
11 MB request body OOM-kills the edge cgroup under mem_limit 96m, and
`docker stop` ends in SIGKILL because a lingering connection blocks Caddy's
eternal grace period while `admin off` leaves no reload endpoint to drain
through.
NO setcap, and the edge Dockerfile lost its only RUN as a result. The
assertion that no layer carries the capability xattr moved to CI, paired
with a control proving the same check FINDS it in the stock image.
Evidence: .evidence/base-image-compat/, .evidence/anonrouter-base-build/

components.role: Terminates customer TLS inside the trust domain. This is the serving path, not an optional one: every request arrives through it
note: SOURCE PINNED AND VERIFIED. Still a RECORDED GAP.
The upstream source is pinned to a full commit SHA, every one of the 34
files was re-hashed against the git object ids in that commit's tree, the
licence was read and confirmed Apache-2.0, and the build inputs were
extracted from the upstream Dockerfile. Re-runnable by
scripts/pin-dstack-ingress-source.ts.
That is half of option A. The other half, rebuilding from these bytes and
matching a deployed digest, is NOT done, so the binding stays NONE. A
source pin says which bytes we intend to build; a binding says the running
image came from them. Only the second is what this gate asks for.
An image IS deployed, at the digest above, named in the MEASURED app_compose
of the content-plane release and pinned in the generated
deploy/phala/docker-compose.prod5-xl.yml. Stated plainly because this entry
once said `pinned.image: null` and gave as its FIRST blocker that 'no image
is deployed to bind to' -- false, and false in the direction that flattered
us, since the component is on the serving path of every request.
THE PIN MOVED 2.2 -> 2.3 ON 2026-08-31, AND IT NARROWS THE GAP RATHER THAN
WIDENING IT. The reason for the move is a feature: 2.2 is single-domain,
and DOMAINS/ROUTING_MAP are what let one attested workload serve the
restored api.anonrouter.ai base URL alongside the api.private launch origin.
It also fixes a version skew this entry did not name. The pinned commit
b1a90408 is dated 2026-07-29 and its own README documents DOMAINS,
ROUTING_MAP and an example naming image 2.3 by the digest below. So the
source this project reviewed was ALREADY NEWER than the 2.2 image it ran:
the recorded gap was not merely 'no rebuild', it was 'a source pin
describing a different release from the one deployed'. Pinning 2.3 makes
the source pin and the deployed digest describe the same upstream release.
HOW THE DIGEST WAS RESOLVED, and it is not a copy from a document. The
Docker Hub registry API was queried READ-ONLY for the tag list and for the
tag-to-digest mapping of both 2.2 and 2.3. 2.2 resolved to the digest this
entry previously carried, which is the control that says the method is
sound; 2.3 resolved to the digest above, and it equals the digest upstream's
own README names at the pinned commit. Two independent sources agreeing is
not a rebuild, and it is not claimed as one.
WHY THE REBUILD DID NOT RUN, restated accurately:
1. There is no public CI to run it in. WO-07 section 2.2 option A
requires the rebuild to happen in our PUBLIC CI under the provenance
policy of section 8.1, so the binding is verifiable by a reader rather
than asserted by whoever ran the build. The workflows are prepared and
inert (.github/workflows/), and the repository they name does not
exist. This is the blocker that matters: a laptop build is a rehearsal,
not a binding, however it turns out.
2. Upstream's build-image.sh additionally requires skopeo, which is not
installed.
A FURTHER RISK NOW THAT THERE IS A TARGET, recorded before it surprises
anyone: the deployed digest is upstream's PUBLISHED image, and upstream
did not necessarily build it from the pinned commit under conditions we
can reproduce. If a faithful rebuild of b1a90408 produces a different
digest, the correct outcome is that the binding stays NONE and the
discrepancy is recorded. A near miss is not a partial pass.
Upstream is a good option-A candidate: the Dockerfile pins its base image
by digest, pins Debian to a snapshot-archive timestamp, pins package
versions in pinned-packages.txt, pins the lego binary by sha256, and sets
deterministic permissions and timestamps.
CORRECTED 2026-09-01 BY MEASUREMENT, AND IT RETRACTS A CLAIM ABOVE.
This entry says pinning 2.3 'makes the source pin and the deployed digest
describe the same upstream release'. That is FALSE, and it was falsifiable
the whole time by a check nobody had run: upstream bakes `git rev-parse HEAD`
into the image at /etc/.GIT_REV, so the source commit is a property of the
artifact rather than a claim about it.
Read out of the deployed image, 2.3 was built from b322d14e (2026-07-28,
'chore(ingress): bump image tag to 2.3'). The pinned commit b1a90408 is
2026-07-29 and is NINE ingress commits later, including substantive changes
to scripts/certman.py and a 310-line test file the deployed image does not
contain. The version skew this entry congratulated itself on closing was
narrowed, not closed. 2.2 records 2b4fbcbc, by the same method.
The new deployedSource field carries that value structurally, and the schema
now requires a REBUILT claim to name it rather than the reviewed commit. A
rebuild of b1a90408 compared against 527c5352 would have been the right
procedure run against the wrong bytes, and it would have reported the
mismatch as a reproducibility failure instead of as a bad pin.
FIRST REBUILD RESULT, AND IT IS NOT A PASS. Building b322d14e with upstream's
own invocation (BuildKit v0.20.2, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0, rewrite-timestamp,
--no-cache, linux/amd64) produced sha256:cd31a96a..., not sha256:527c5352...
Ten of eleven layers are byte-identical, including the lego layer, the scripts
layer and the .GIT_REV layer, and the image configuration matches in created,
architecture, os, Env, Entrypoint, Cmd, WorkingDir, User and every history
entry. The one differing layer differs by exactly three directory entries
present only in the rebuild: /root, /root/.cache and /root/.cache/rosetta,
written by Rosetta 2 on the Apple Silicon host that ran it.
That remains a RECORDED GAP and the binding stays NONE. An explained
difference is still a difference, and this entry already committed to that
outcome before the measurement existed. What it does establish is that the
residual delta is attributable to the builder rather than to the source, so a
native linux/amd64 run is worth doing rather than hopeless.
Blocker 1 above is now half-answered: .github/workflows/dstack-ingress-rebuild.yml
is that public CI. It reads the source commit out of the deployed image rather
than trusting this file, runs on ubuntu-latest so no emulation is involved, and
compares with scripts/provenance/compare-oci-images.ts, which lists every
difference file by file. It cannot run until the public repository has it.
Evidence: .evidence/dstack-escrow/ingress-rebuild-comparison.json.
WHAT PRODUCTION ACTUALLY PULLS, now recorded structurally in `runtime`.
This entry's `pinned` field names the upstream image, and the generated public
README turned that into the sentence 'Deployed at dstacktee/dstack-ingress:2.3'.
Production has not pulled that image at boot for some time: the measured
prod5-xl compose names ghcr.io/anonrouter/anonrouter-dstack-ingress@sha256:bb6fbf4f...,
an AnonRouter image built FROM the pinned digest.
That is better than the README implied, and the README being wrong is the
problem regardless of which direction it was wrong in. A checkable sentence in
a transparency document that does not survive checking is worse than no
sentence, and this one was generated, so it would have been regenerated wrong
every release until the field existed to say otherwise.
BINDING ESTABLISHED 2026-09-01. STATUS NONE -> REBUILT.
AnonRouter's public CI rebuilt b322d14e on ubuntu-latest, natively linux/amd64
with no emulation, and produced
That is the deployed digest, byte for byte: 11 of 11 layers identical, zero
changed paths, zero paths on either side alone.
This settles the near match recorded above. The local rebuild differed only by
three Rosetta 2 cache directories, and the hypothesis that the residual delta
belonged to the builder rather than the source was correct. The honest
refusal to call that a pass is what made the native run worth doing.
The rebuilt image is published at
ghcr.io/anonrouter/mirror/dstack-ingress-rebuilt@sha256:527c5352... and carries
three signed objects at that digest: a keyless cosign signature, a SLSA v1
build-provenance attestation and an SPDX SBOM attestation.
VERIFY IT YOURSELF, and note which identity string works:
cosign verify \
--certificate-identity 'https://github.com/anonrouter/confidential-content-plane/.github/workflows/dstack-ingress-rebuild.yml@refs/heads/main' \
--certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' \
ghcr.io/anonrouter/mirror/dstack-ingress-rebuilt@sha256:527c53523b9226782a11dbd800a3ff55e8a1f0b88e6224e8f7e4db7419769fbe
The first signed run published the bare `job_workflow_ref` claim as the
certificate identity. It does not verify: Fulcio's SAN carries an
https://github.com/ prefix the claim omits. Found by verifying our own
signature from outside CI, which is the only way that surfaces, because the
run was green and the signature was real and the identity was unusable.
builderWorkflowRef above is the form cosign accepts.

runtime.note: Built from the pinned upstream digest by deploy/phala/images/ingress-delegated/Dockerfile, which adds one Route53 delegation write and three pinned edits to upstream's dns01.sh and certman.py. Production therefore pulls nothing from docker.io at boot; the upstream artifact is a build-time dependency. Named in the measured deploy/phala/docker-compose.prod5-xl.yml.

components.role: Base image of the content-plane image; runs every line of code that handles plaintext
note: PROBLEM 1, MUTABLE REFERENCE: CLOSED. Every plaintext-capable build
input now pins the linux/amd64 IMAGE MANIFEST digest above. Not the tag,
which moves, and not the multi-arch index digest, which is immutable but
still resolves to a different image per builder architecture. The index
digest is recorded alongside for traceability, not used as the pin.
The digest was resolved by walking index bytes -> amd64 entry -> child
manifest bytes -> config blob, recomputing every hash locally rather than
trusting a registry header, and the config blob confirms linux/amd64.
Enforced by tests/unit/base-image-pin.test.ts.
PROBLEM 2, CONTENTS UNVERIFIED: OPEN, and this is why the binding is
still NONE. A pinned digest makes the build reproducible; it says nothing
about what is inside the image. WO-07 section 2.2 applies to base images
for exactly this reason. Closing the first half must not be mistaken for
closing the second.
Option A here means rebuilding the Debian-based Node image from the
nodejs/docker-node Dockerfile and its Debian base, which transitively
means trusting Debian's own archive. Option B means verifying provenance
that Docker Official Images do not currently publish in a form we can pin
to a single upstream identity. Neither is closed by this change.
MEASURED 2026-09-02, AND THE RESULT IS UNUSUALLY CLEAN.
AnonRouter's public CI replayed docker-library's recorded invocation for
this exact digest, natively on linux/amd64, three times, with every argument
read out of the deployed image's own SLSA statement: nodejs/docker-node at
bc0a422b, path 22/bookworm-slim, the debian:bookworm-slim parent resolved to
oisupport/staging-amd64@sha256:362e6422, the tianon/buildkit:0.16 frontend by
digest. The replay was handed the deployed manifest's own annotations too,
which makes the test maximally favourable.
Two IDENTICAL invocations, minutes apart with a cold cache, produced
sha256:6babfba1... and sha256:c1d12a97..., which are different images. The
published recipe is therefore not deterministic, so no replay of it can match
a fixed digest, whoever runs the replay. Scope is in claimScope below.
WHAT DIFFERED BETWEEN THOSE TWO RUNS IS THE WHOLE FINDING, and it is four
files: /var/log/dpkg.log, /var/log/alternatives.log, /var/log/apt/history.log
and /var/log/apt/term.log. Zero paths present on one side only. Zero other
content changes anywhere in 5,759 scanned files. Every one of those four is a
log apt and dpkg wrote and the image then shipped, recording WHEN the build
ran rather than what it built. The deployed image's dpkg.log carries 1,052
such stamps and begins '2026-08-05 00:49:00 startup archives unpack'.
So the Node recipe is deterministic in every respect except its own clock,
and the clock is in file CONTENT where no normalisation flag reaches it. That
is a much more specific finding than 'it did not reproduce', and it is the
one that says what a fix would have to do.
Against the deployed image the rebuild differs in nine paths and every one is
a clock or a cache: the four logs above, /var/log/apt/eipp.log.xz,
/var/cache/debconf/config.dat-old, templates.dat-old,
/var/cache/ldconfig/aux-cache, and /etc/shadow, whose last-changed field is a
day count. Notably NOT the Debian archive: no package content moved, which is
the opposite of what happened to the Alpine-based caddy base.
The SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH branch was tested and also failed
(sha256:116a5d09...), so neither half of that fork is left as an untested
excuse.
NO QUALIFYING SIGNATURE EXISTED ON 2026-09-02, MEASURED. No OCI referrer on the child or the index,
no cosign .sig sibling tag, no GitHub attestation under docker-library, and
no Sigstore transparency-log entry over this digest at all.

compatibility.comparedAgainst: the base the component runs today, same source, same policy

integratedIn: the production stage of the Dockerfile generated by scripts/export-content-plane.ts
note: UNDEPLOYED CANDIDATE, INTEGRATED IN SOURCE. It proves nothing about the
digest above.
BUILT FROM scratch, for the same reason as the caddy one: the first version
was FROM debian:bookworm-slim and inherited the very provenance gap it was
supposed to close. The rootfs is assembled from a Node release tarball
pinned by the sha256 nodejs.org signs and Debian packages pinned by sha256
values that also appear in the Packages index Debian's OpenPGP-signed
Release covers. 322 MB became 56 MB.
WHAT IT NEEDS WAS MEASURED. `ldd` over the node binary and over every native
module the production set installs -- onnxruntime, sharp, libvips-cpp,
argon2 -- names exactly libc6, libgcc-s1 and libstdc++6. yarn, apt, dpkg and
/etc/shadow are absent by choice; the last of those removes an
irreproducibility by construction, since the deployed image records the
build DAY in its last-changed field.
THE PINS WERE CORROBORATED AGAINST THE ARTIFACT IN SERVICE. The node binary
in the pinned tarball hashes to 3517c2df..., byte-identical to
/usr/local/bin/node inside node:22-bookworm-slim@sha256:a17d50af.
COMPATIBILITY WAS MEASURED ON THE REAL IMAGE. The harness builds the actual
content plane on both bases and compares: every production dependency loads,
sharp encodes, onnxruntime loads, aws_signing_helper runs, uid is 1000:1000,
the rootfs is read-only, /tmp is writable, DNS resolves to the same address
family, the trust store holds the same 150 roots, and the application boots
and answers /healthz. 13 of 13 identical. A base with an emptied CA bundle
is the control the matrix must detect, and does.
TWO DIFFERENCES WERE FOUND AND FIXED RATHER THAN WAIVED. ca-certificates
pinned from `bookworm main` gave 142 roots against the deployed image's 150
from bookworm-security; and a missing /etc/gai.conf made
dns.lookup('localhost') return 127.0.0.1 where the deployed image returns
::1. Both would have been invisible to a version print.
ONE PRE-EXISTING FINDING, reproducing on the stock base: the content plane
exits 143 on SIGTERM rather than handling it and exiting 0, so an in-flight
request is dropped on every deploy rather than drained. An application
change, not a base-image one.
WHAT IS STILL UNPROVEN, recorded rather than left to be discovered: the
chain does not bottom out at nothing. It bottoms out at Debian's archive
signature over the .deb bytes, which is a real upstream signature over exact
content and is NOT the same shape as this project's option B bar, because
the identity is an OpenPGP archive key rather than a pinned certificate
identity and OIDC issuer. It is recorded as a trust dependency, not counted
as a binding.
